title: SOLID Principles: Five Smells and Their Fixes
oneLiner: Each principle as a before and after in C#, plus the code smell that tells you it is being broken.
keyTakeaway: SOLID is a set of reasons code becomes hard to change, not a checklist to satisfy. Learn the smell first (a class that changes for two reasons, a switch that grows with every feature, an override that throws, an interface full of NotImplementedException, a `new` buried inside business logic) and the fix usually follows on its own.
explanation:
SOLID is five principles Robert Martin collected for object oriented design: Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. Each one names a specific way code resists change. Most design patterns in the rest of this track exist because of one of them: Strategy is Open/Closed applied, Adapter rescues you from a Dependency Inversion mismatch, and Decorator lets you add behavior without editing a class that already works.

Pick a principle below. Each one shows a small C# class that breaks it, the refactored version (restructured without changing what it does), and the smell you would notice in a real code review. The smell is the part worth memorizing: in an interview you are rarely asked to recite a definition, but you are often handed code and asked what is wrong with it.

A word of balance: every principle can be overapplied. Splitting a 40 line class into six interfaces with one method each is not good design, it is indirection. Apply a principle when you can name the change it protects you from.
